# Circular Motion & Trigonometry

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Describe circular motion using angle and radius.
- Set up and solve right-triangle trigonometry problems.
- Evaluate trigonometric functions using the unit circle.
- Recognize core trigonometric identities.

---

## Circular Motion Basics

Many environmental processes have a **cyclical** pattern — they repeat in a predictable way over time. We could link this to the second hand of an angular clock that moves across the clock face at a constant speed, eventually repeating its path each minute. Seasonal daylight hours, tidal height, and the rotation of a wind turbine blade all share this underlying structure: a quantity that sweeps through an angle at a steady rate and returns to where it started.

```{r circle-to-sine, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Drag the slider or press Play. As the point sweeps around the circle at a steady rate, its height traces out the sine curve."}
library(plotly)

step <- 5                         # degrees per frame
deg  <- seq(0, 360, by = step)    # frame values (integers keep frames in order)
cx   <- -1.5                      # circle centre sits left of the graph

# Fixed unit circle (no frame, so it stays put in every frame)
tt   <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200)
circ <- data.frame(x = cx + cos(tt), y = sin(tt))

# Where the point is at each frame: on the circle and on the curve
pt <- data.frame(deg = deg, th = deg * pi / 180)
pt$px <- cx + cos(pt$th)
pt$py <- sin(pt$th)

# Sine curve drawn so far: frame k holds every point from 0 up to angle k
trace <- do.call(rbind, lapply(deg, function(d) {
  th <- seq(0, d, by = step) * pi / 180
  data.frame(deg = d, x = th, y = sin(th))
}))

blue   <- "#003F7F"   # high contrast against white
orange <- "#8A3B00"

plot_ly(height = 430) |>
  add_paths(data = circ, x = ~x, y = ~y,
            line = list(color = "black", width = 2),
            hoverinfo = "skip", name = "Circle") |>
  # radius: centre to the moving point
  add_segments(data = pt, frame = ~deg,
               x = cx, y = 0, xend = ~px, yend = ~py,
               line = list(color = blue, width = 2),
               hoverinfo = "skip", name = "Radius") |>
  # connector: same height on the circle and on the curve
  add_segments(data = pt, frame = ~deg,
               x = ~px, y = ~py, xend = ~th, yend = ~py,
               line = list(color = "black", width = 1, dash = "dash"),
               hoverinfo = "skip", name = "Same height") |>
  add_lines(data = trace, frame = ~deg, x = ~x, y = ~y,
            line = list(color = orange, width = 3),
            hoverinfo = "skip", name = "sin(θ)") |>
  add_markers(data = pt, frame = ~deg, x = ~px, y = ~py,
              marker = list(color = blue, size = 12),
              hoverinfo = "skip", name = "Point on circle") |>
  add_markers(data = pt, frame = ~deg, x = ~th, y = ~py,
              marker = list(color = orange, size = 12),
              text = ~sprintf("θ = %d°<br>height = %.2f", deg, py),
              hoverinfo = "text", name = "Point on curve") |>
  layout(
    showlegend = FALSE,
    xaxis = list(
      title = "Angle θ (radians)",
      range = c(cx - 1.2, 2 * pi + 0.3),
      tickvals = c(0, pi / 2, pi, 3 * pi / 2, 2 * pi),
      ticktext = c("0", "π/2", "π", "3π/2", "2π"),
      zeroline = FALSE
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Height",
      range = c(-1.3, 1.3),
      scaleanchor = "x",          # keeps the circle round
      tickvals = c(-1, 0, 1),
      zeroline = TRUE
    )
  ) |>
  animation_opts(frame = 120, transition = 0, redraw = FALSE) |>
  animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "Angle: ", suffix = "°",
                                       font = list(color = "black", size = 16))) |>
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```


If an object moves around a circle of radius \(r\) at a constant **angular speed** \(\omega\) (radians per unit time), the angle swept out after time \(t\) is:

$$
\theta(t) = \omega t
$$

and, from Chapter 7, the arc length traveled is \(s = r\theta = r\omega t\).

::: promptbox

**Two Kinds of Speed**

A large wind turbine blade and a small one rotate at the same angular speed (say, one full rotation every 4 seconds). Which blade's *tip* is moving faster through the air — the long one or the short one? Why, even though their angular speed is identical?

<div class="writein"></div>
:::

### Worked Example: A Turbine Blade Tip Speed

A wind turbine blade is 40 m long and completes one full rotation every 4 seconds.

**Step 1 — Find the angular speed.** One full rotation is \(2\pi\) radians, completed in 4 seconds:

$$
\omega = \frac{2\pi \text{ radians}}{4 \text{ s}} = \frac{\pi}{2} \text{ radians/s}
$$

**Step 2 — Find the linear (tip) speed using \(s = r\theta\), applied as a rate.** Since \(s = r\omega t\), the tip's speed is \(r\omega\):

$$
v = r\omega = 40 \times \frac{\pi}{2} = 20\pi \approx 62.8 \text{ m/s}
$$

**Step 3 — Interpret.** The blade tip moves at roughly 63 m/s — over 225 km/h (140 mph) — even though the whole blade completes the same *angular* rotation as any point closer to the hub. Points farther from the center cover more linear distance in the same rotation, which is exactly the intuition from the prompt box above.

```{r trig-same-angle-different-arcs, fig.cap="Same angular speed, different linear speeds. In one second, every point on the blade turns through the same angle, \u03c0/2 radians. A point 20 m from the hub travels an arc of 20 \u00d7 \u03c0/2 \u2248 31.4 m; the tip, 40 m out, travels 40 \u00d7 \u03c0/2 \u2248 62.8 m. Twice the radius, twice the distance, in the same time.", fig.alt="Diagram of a turbine hub at the center with a blade drawn at two moments one second apart: first pointing to the right, then rotated a quarter turn counterclockwise to point straight up. Two arcs show the paths traveled during that second. A short inner arc at radius 20 meters is labeled about 31.4 meters. A long outer arc at radius 40 meters, traced by the blade tip, is labeled about 62.8 meters. A small arc at the hub between the two blade positions is labeled pi over 2 radians in 1 second.", cache=FALSE, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)

blue   <- "#003F7F"
orange <- "#8A3B00"

th   <- seq(0, pi / 2, length.out = 120)
arcs <- rbind(
  data.frame(x = 20 * cos(th), y = 20 * sin(th), r = "20 m"),
  data.frame(x = 40 * cos(th), y = 40 * sin(th), r = "40 m")
)
ang <- data.frame(x = 6 * cos(th), y = 6 * sin(th))

ggplot() +
  # blade at t = 0 and t = 1 s
  annotate("segment", x = 0, y = 0, xend = 40, yend = 0, color = "grey45",
           linewidth = 2.2, lineend = "round") +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, y = 0, xend = 0, yend = 40, color = "black",
           linewidth = 2.2, lineend = "round") +
  annotate("text", x = 41, y = -3, hjust = 0, size = 3.8, color = "grey25", label = "t = 0") +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 42.5, hjust = 0, size = 3.8, label = "t = 1 s") +
  geom_path(data = arcs, aes(x, y, group = r, color = r), linewidth = 1.6,
            linetype = "dashed",
            arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
  geom_path(data = ang, aes(x, y), linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 7.5, y = 7.5, hjust = 0, size = 3.8,
           label = "\u03c0/2 rad\nin 1 s", lineheight = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 20 * cos(pi / 4) + 1.5, y = 20 * sin(pi / 4) + 1.5, hjust = 0,
           size = 4.1, color = blue, label = "r = 20 m:\n\u2248 31.4 m", lineheight = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 40 * cos(pi / 4) + 1.5, y = 40 * sin(pi / 4) + 1.5, hjust = 0,
           size = 4.1, color = orange, label = "Tip, r = 40 m:\n\u2248 62.8 m", lineheight = 0.9) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = 0, size = 5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`20 m` = blue, `40 m` = orange), guide = "none") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-3, 56), ylim = c(-5, 46)) +
  theme_void()
```

## Right-Triangle Trigonometry

For a right triangle with one acute angle \(\theta\), the three basic trigonometric ratios relate the angle to the triangle's side lengths:

$$
\sin(\theta) = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \qquad \cos(\theta) = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \qquad \tan(\theta) = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}
$$

```{r trig-right-triangle-labels, fig.cap="Naming the sides of a right triangle relative to the angle θ. The hypotenuse is always the longest side, across from the right angle. Opposite and adjacent depend on which acute angle you are using: opposite is across from θ, adjacent is the leg that touches θ.", fig.alt="A right triangle with the right angle at the lower right, marked with a small square. The angle theta is at the lower left, marked with a small arc. The bottom horizontal side, touching theta, is labeled adjacent. The vertical side on the right, across from theta, is labeled opposite. The slanted side joining the lower left to the top right is labeled hypotenuse. Beside the triangle the three ratios are written: sine theta equals opposite over hypotenuse, cosine theta equals adjacent over hypotenuse, tangent theta equals opposite over adjacent.", fig.height=3.6, cache=FALSE, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)

blue   <- "#003F7F"
orange <- "#8A3B00"

W <- 4; H <- 3
a <- atan2(H, W)
arc <- data.frame(x = 0.7 * cos(seq(0, a, length.out = 50)),
                  y = 0.7 * sin(seq(0, a, length.out = 50)))

ggplot() +
  annotate("polygon", x = c(0, W, W), y = c(0, 0, H), fill = "grey95", color = NA) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, y = 0, xend = W, yend = 0, color = blue, linewidth = 1.5) +
  annotate("segment", x = W, y = 0, xend = W, yend = H, color = orange, linewidth = 1.5) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, y = 0, xend = W, yend = H, color = "black", linewidth = 1.5) +
  annotate("path", x = c(W - 0.3, W - 0.3, W), y = c(0, 0.3, 0.3)) +
  geom_path(data = arc, aes(x, y)) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.85, y = 0.28, hjust = 0, size = 5, label = "θ") +
  annotate("text", x = W / 2, y = -0.3, size = 4.6, color = blue, label = "adjacent") +
  annotate("text", x = W + 0.15, y = H / 2, hjust = 0, size = 4.6, color = orange,
           label = "opposite") +
  annotate("text", x = W / 2 - 0.35, y = H / 2 + 0.3, size = 4.6, angle = a * 180 / pi,
           label = "hypotenuse") +
  annotate("text", x = W + 1.9, y = c(2.4, 1.6, 0.8), hjust = 0, size = 4.4,
           label = c("sin(θ) = opposite / hypotenuse",
                     "cos(θ) = adjacent / hypotenuse",
                     "tan(θ) = opposite / adjacent")) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-0.3, 10.6), ylim = c(-0.6, 3.3)) +
  theme_void()
```

### Worked Example: Estimating Canopy Height

An ecologist stands 30 m from the base of a tree and measures the angle of elevation to its top as \(35°\).

**Step 1 — Identify the triangle.** The horizontal distance (30 m) is the side *adjacent* to the angle; the tree height is the side *opposite* the angle.

**Step 2 — Choose the ratio that relates opposite and adjacent.**

$$
\tan(35°) = \frac{\text{height}}{30}
$$

**Step 3 — Solve for height.**

$$
\text{height} = 30\tan(35°) \approx 30(0.7002) \approx 21.0 \text{ m}
$$

**Step 4 — Interpret.** The tree is approximately 21 meters tall — measured without ever needing to climb it or use a direct measuring tool, just an angle and a horizontal distance.

```{r trig-canopy-height, fig.cap="The canopy-height measurement as a right triangle. The 30 m of level ground is adjacent to the 35° angle of elevation and the tree's height is opposite it, so height = 30 tan(35°) ≈ 21.0 m. As drawn, the angle is measured from ground level at the observer's position.", fig.alt="Side-view diagram of a right triangle on level ground. On the left, a small marker shows the observer's position. On the right stands a vertical tree trunk with a rounded canopy on top. The ground between them is labeled 30 meters, adjacent. The tree's height, from the ground to the top of the canopy, is labeled height approximately 21.0 meters, opposite. A dashed line of sight runs from the observer up to the treetop, labeled hypotenuse, line of sight. At the observer, an arc between the ground and the line of sight is labeled 35 degrees. A small square marks the right angle at the base of the tree.", fig.height=4, cache=FALSE, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)

blue   <- "#003F7F"
orange <- "#8A3B00"
green  <- "#1a5e3a"

d <- 30; a <- 35 * pi / 180; h <- d * tan(a)
arc <- data.frame(x = 5 * cos(seq(0, a, length.out = 50)),
                  y = 5 * sin(seq(0, a, length.out = 50)))
crown <- data.frame(x = d + 4.2 * cos(seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 100)),
                    y = h - 4 + 4.2 * sin(seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 100)))

ggplot() +
  annotate("segment", x = -3, xend = 38, y = 0, yend = 0, color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.8) +
  # tree
  annotate("segment", x = d, xend = d, y = 0, yend = h - 6, color = "#5a3a1a", linewidth = 3) +
  geom_polygon(data = crown, aes(x, y), fill = green, alpha = 0.35, color = green) +
  # triangle
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = d, y = 0, yend = 0, color = blue, linewidth = 1.5) +
  annotate("segment", x = d + 6, xend = d + 6, y = 0, yend = h, color = orange,
           linewidth = 1.2, arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.2, "cm"))) +
  annotate("segment", x = d, xend = d + 6, y = h, yend = h, color = "grey50",
           linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = d, y = 0, yend = h, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("path", x = c(d - 1.2, d - 1.2, d), y = c(0, 1.2, 1.2)) +
  geom_path(data = arc, aes(x, y)) +
  annotate("text", x = 5.8, y = 1.6, hjust = 0, size = 4.3, label = "35°") +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = 0, shape = 17, size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = -2.2, size = 3.9, label = "Observer") +
  annotate("text", x = d / 2, y = -2.2, size = 4.2, color = blue,
           label = "30 m (adjacent)") +
  annotate("text", x = d + 6.8, y = h / 2, hjust = 0, size = 4.2, color = orange,
           label = "height ≈ 21.0 m\n(opposite)", lineheight = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = d / 2 - 2.5, y = h / 2 + 2.5, size = 4, angle = 35,
           label = "line of sight (hypotenuse)") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-4, 50), ylim = c(-3.5, 24)) +
  theme_void()
```

### Concept Check: Right-Triangle Trig Setup {-}

**1. In the canopy example, why was tangent the right ratio to use, rather than sine or cosine?**

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal answer</strong></summary>

Tangent relates the **opposite** and **adjacent** sides, and those are exactly the two sides we knew or wanted (adjacent = 30 m horizontal distance, opposite = the unknown height). Sine and cosine both involve the hypotenuse, which we didn't know here.

</details>

**2. A ramp rises 2 m over a horizontal run of 15 m. What angle does the ramp make with the ground?**

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal answer</strong></summary>

\(\tan(\theta) = \dfrac{2}{15} \Rightarrow \theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{15}\right) \approx 7.6°\).

</details>

## The Unit Circle

The **unit circle** is a circle of radius 1 centered at the origin. For any angle \(\theta\) (measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis), the point where the angle's ray crosses the unit circle has coordinates \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\). This is what lets sine and cosine be defined for *any* angle, not just acute angles inside a right triangle.

```{r trig-unit-circle-coordinates, fig.cap="On the unit circle, the point at angle θ has coordinates (cos θ, sin θ). Left angle: θ = 50°, where both coordinates are positive and the right triangle has legs cos θ and sin θ with hypotenuse 1. Right angle: θ = 140°, beyond any right triangle's acute angle, where the point lies left of the y-axis and cos θ is negative. The coordinate definition works for both.", fig.width=8.5, fig.height=4, fig.alt="Two side-by-side unit circles, each centered at the origin with radius 1. In each, an arc from the positive x-axis shows the angle, a radius goes to a marked point on the circle, and dashed lines drop from the point to the x-axis. Left circle, theta equals 50 degrees: the point is in the upper right, the horizontal leg along the x-axis is labeled cosine theta and is positive, the vertical leg is labeled sine theta, and the radius is labeled 1. The point is labeled (cosine theta, sine theta). Right circle, theta equals 140 degrees: the point is in the upper left, the horizontal leg extends to the left of the origin and is labeled cosine theta, negative, and the vertical leg is labeled sine theta, positive.", cache=FALSE, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)

blue   <- "#003F7F"
orange <- "#8A3B00"

lv <- c("θ = 50°", "θ = 140°")
ths <- c(50, 140) * pi / 180

tt   <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 300)
circ <- do.call(rbind, lapply(lv, function(p) data.frame(x = cos(tt), y = sin(tt), panel = p)))
arcs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(i) {
  s <- seq(0, ths[i], length.out = 80)
  data.frame(x = 0.25 * cos(s), y = 0.25 * sin(s), panel = lv[i])
}))
pts <- data.frame(panel = lv, x = cos(ths), y = sin(ths))
lab <- data.frame(panel = lv,
                  cx = cos(ths) / 2, cy = -0.12,
                  clab = c("cos θ", "cos θ (negative)"),
                  sx = cos(ths) + c(-0.06, 0.06), sy = sin(ths) / 4,
                  sh = c(1, 0),
                  px = cos(ths) + c(0.06, -0.06), py = sin(ths) + 0.12,
                  ph = c(0, 1))

for (d in c("circ", "arcs", "pts", "lab")) {
  tmp <- get(d); tmp$panel <- factor(tmp$panel, levels = lv); assign(d, tmp)
}

ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_path(data = circ, aes(x, y), color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_path(data = arcs, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_segment(data = pts, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = x, yend = y), color = "black",
               linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_segment(data = pts, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = x, yend = 0), color = blue,
               linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_segment(data = pts, aes(x = x, y = 0, xend = x, yend = y), color = orange,
               linewidth = 1.6, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = pts, aes(x, y), size = 3.6) +
  geom_text(data = pts, aes(x = x / 2 + c(-0.08, 0.08), y = y / 2 + 0.08, label = "1"),
            size = 4.2) +
  geom_text(data = lab, aes(cx, cy, label = clab), color = blue, size = 3.9) +
  geom_text(data = lab, aes(sx, sy, label = "sin θ", hjust = sh), color = orange,
            size = 3.9) +
  geom_text(data = lab, aes(px, py, label = "(cos θ, sin θ)", hjust = ph),
            size = 3.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-1.45, 1.45), ylim = c(-1.15, 1.25)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

**Key standard angles** (in radians, with degrees noted):

| \(\theta\) | \(0\) | \(\pi/6\) (30°) | \(\pi/4\) (45°) | \(\pi/3\) (60°) | \(\pi/2\) (90°) |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| \(\cos\theta\) | \(1\) | \(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) | \(\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\) | \(\dfrac12\) | \(0\) |
| \(\sin\theta\) | \(0\) | \(\dfrac12\) | \(\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\) | \(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) | \(1\) |

## Core Trig Identities (Introduction)

The single most important trig identity comes directly from the unit circle being, well, a circle of radius 1 — so every point \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\) on it satisfies the circle equation from Chapter 2 with \(r=1\):

$$
\sin^2(\theta) + \cos^2(\theta) = 1
$$

This is the **Pythagorean identity**, and it holds for *every* angle \(\theta\), not just the standard ones in the table above.

```{r trig-pythagorean-identity, fig.cap="The Pythagorean identity for every angle at once. As θ runs from 0 to 2π, sin²(θ) and cos²(θ) each rise and fall between 0 and 1, but whenever one goes up the other comes down by exactly the same amount. Stacked together, they always fill the band up to exactly 1.", fig.height=3.6, fig.alt="Stacked area chart over theta from 0 to 2 pi. The lower layer, in blue, is sine squared of theta: it starts at 0, rises to 1 at pi over 2, falls to 0 at pi, rises to 1 at 3 pi over 2, and returns to 0 at 2 pi. The upper layer, in orange, is cosine squared of theta, stacked on top. It is thickest where the blue layer is thinnest. The top edge of the stack is a flat line at exactly 1 across the whole graph, labeled sine squared plus cosine squared equals 1.", cache=FALSE, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)

blue   <- "#003F7F"
orange <- "#8A3B00"

th <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 400)
df <- rbind(
  data.frame(th = th, v = cos(th)^2, part = "cos²(θ)"),
  data.frame(th = th, v = sin(th)^2, part = "sin²(θ)")
)
df$part <- factor(df$part, levels = c("cos²(θ)", "sin²(θ)"))

ggplot(df, aes(th, v, fill = part)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.85, color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("label", x = pi, y = 1.08, size = 4, label.size = 0, fill = "white",
           label = "sin²(θ) + cos²(θ) = 1 for every θ") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(orange, blue)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, pi / 2, pi, 3 * pi / 2, 2 * pi),
                     labels = c("0", "π/2", "π", "3π/2", "2π")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1.15)) +
  labs(x = "θ (radians)", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

### Concept Check: Unit Circle Values {-}

**1. Using the unit circle, what is \(\cos(\pi/3)\)?**

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal answer</strong></summary>

\(\cos(\pi/3) = \dfrac12\).

</details>

**2. If \(\sin(\theta) = 0.6\), use the Pythagorean identity to find \(\cos(\theta)\), assuming \(\theta\) is in the first quadrant (so cosine is positive).**

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal answer</strong></summary>

\(\cos^2(\theta) = 1 - 0.6^2 = 1-0.36=0.64 \Rightarrow \cos(\theta) = \sqrt{0.64} = 0.8\).

</details>

## Practice: Modeling a Rotational/Cyclical Process

### What Are You Practicing?

Connecting angular speed to linear (tip) speed, solving right-triangle problems for an unknown side or angle, and applying the Pythagorean identity.

### How to Approach These Problems

1. For rotational speed problems: find angular speed first (angle swept ÷ time), then multiply by radius for linear speed.
2. For right-triangle problems: label which sides are opposite/adjacent relative to the angle you're using, then choose the matching ratio.
3. For identity problems: substitute the known value into \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\) and solve for the unknown, keeping track of sign based on which quadrant the angle is in.

### Practice Problems

**1.** A buoy bobs in a circular tidal eddy of radius 5 m, completing one loop every 20 seconds. Find its angular speed and its linear speed.

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal solution</strong></summary>

\(\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{20} = \dfrac{\pi}{10}\) rad/s. Linear speed: \(v = r\omega = 5\times\dfrac{\pi}{10} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57\) m/s.

</details>

**2.** A drone hovers and measures the angle of depression to a wildlife carcass on the ground as \(50°\), from a horizontal distance of 12 m. How high is the drone?

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal solution</strong></summary>

\(\tan(50°) = \dfrac{\text{height}}{12} \Rightarrow \text{height} = 12\tan(50°) \approx 12(1.19) \approx 14.3\) m.

</details>
